SOMA: Continuous Monitoring and Intervention for System Two Reasoning with System One Models

Ruizhi Qian    Lei Shi    Tianyu Hu    Bo Yan    Song Wang    Yu Tian Affiliation: University of Central Florida Affiliation: ru282875@ucf.edu, le779457@ucf.edu, ti721494@ucf.edu Affiliation: bo949643@ucf.edu, song.wang@ucf.edu, yu.tian2@ucf.edu
Abstract

Reasoning models often run into problems without noticing them, even when symptoms are visible in their own text. In humans, metacognition separates monitoring from control: fast, intuitive signals keep watch while slow, deliberate reasoning unfolds and help decide whether to continue, change course, or stop. System One (S1) decision models, such as Jev, are a natural candidate for this role: they return a calibrated probability for a natural-language question about a text in one fast call, yet they are used only as gates before reasoning. We introduce SOMA (System One Metacognitive Awareness), in which an S1 model continuously monitors a System Two (S2) reasoning model and intervenes when needed. SOMA has three layers: a scenario layer states each objective in natural language with predefined actions, an awareness layer lets S1 judge whether the described behavior appears, and a control layer accumulates these judgments, first reminds S2, and takes over only if the behavior persists. Sharing one S1 model and one controller across tasks, without training, SOMA addresses two different failures on two reasoning models: on overthinking, it cuts reasoning tokens by up to 36% while improving average accuracy, and on unanswerable questions, it raises abstention from 70.5% to 87.2%.

1 Introduction

Reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen3 solve problems through long chains of thought (Guo et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025), yet they often run into problems without noticing them, even when the symptoms are visible in their own text. They keep re-verifying an answer they have already confirmed (Chen et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2025), circle back to the same doubts, or state that a problem is missing information and still force a definite answer (Fan et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026). The trace already shows what has gone wrong, but what is lacking is that nothing notices it while the reasoning is still under way.

Human reasoning suggests such an observer. Research on metacognition distinguishes the monitoring of one’s own thinking from its control (Flavell, 1979; Nelson and Narens, 1990): fast, intuitive signals, such as a feeling of rightness or a sensed conflict, accompany slow deliberation and help decide whether it continues, changes course, or stops (Thompson et al., 2011; De Neys and Glumicic, 2008; Ackerman and Thompson, 2017).

Recent System One decision models are a natural candidate for this monitoring role. Exemplified by Jev (Almeida, 2026), they take a text and a natural-language question about it and return a calibrated probability in a single fast call (TypeSafe AI, 2026). Following dual-process accounts (Kahneman, 2011; Evans and Stanovich, 2013), we call these models System One (S1) and reasoning models System Two (S2), as functional labels for fast judgment and slow deliberation.

Two limitations of this design motivate our work. First, S1 models are used only as gates before reasoning begins. Jev’s documentation, for instance, includes an example that uses it to escalate doubtful cases to a reasoning model (TypeSafe AI, 2026) (Figure 1(a)). Once S2 starts, S1 falls silent, and a trace of tens of thousands of tokens unfolds without a fast monitor. Second, existing remedies for these reasoning problems are tailored to one scenario at a time: each ties a dedicated signal, such as trial-answer confidence, answer agreement or a hidden-state probe, to a single action (Yang et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2026; Xie et al., 2026), and many require training or white-box access to the model (Aggarwal and Welleck, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2026). Each new problem thus calls for a new mechanism.

To address both gaps, we introduce SOMA (System One Metacognitive Awareness), in which an S1 model monitors S2 throughout generation and intervenes when needed (Figure 1(b)). SOMA has three layers. The scenario layer states an objective in natural language and lists the actions allowed. The awareness layer asks S1 whether that behavior appears in the trace. The control layer accumulates these judgments, reminds S2 first, and takes over only if the behavior persists. We instantiate SOMA for overthinking and unanswerable questions, which share the same S1 model, controller and system prompt and differ only in their monitors. Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose using S1 decision models as continuous monitors of S2 reasoning rather than gates before it, and introduce SOMA, which separates supervision into scenario, awareness and control layers so that a new objective requires only a natural-language specification.

  • •

    We design a remind-first, take-over-on-persistent-evidence controller with a cumulative log-odds rule, and a calibration procedure that limits the harm of irreversible takeovers.

  • •

    With a single black-box S1 and no training, SOMA reduces reasoning tokens on overthinking by 36% and 16% without lowering average accuracy, and raises abstention on unanswerable questions by 17 and 21 points on two reasoning models.

2 Related Work

2.1 Dual-Process Reasoning and Metacognition

Dual-process theories distinguish fast, intuitive judgments from slow, deliberate reasoning (Sloman, 1996; Kahneman, 2011; Evans and Stanovich, 2013). Metacognitive accounts further distinguish monitoring from control: signals such as confidence and detected conflict can determine whether deliberation continues, changes course, or stops (Flavell, 1979; Nelson and Narens, 1990; Ackerman and Thompson, 2017; De Neys and Glumicic, 2008; Thompson et al., 2011; Ackerman, 2014). We use this relationship as a functional analogy for an S1 model that observes an S2 reasoning trace and supplies judgments to a controller.

2.2 System One Decision Models

This distinction has recently reappeared in model design. System One decision models return typed, probabilistic judgments instead of free-form text. Jev was an early public example; related models now include CLM, Laya, OpenAI’s Decisions API (gpt-6-luna), and Microsoft-Decision-1 (Almeida, 2026; TypeSafe AI, 2026; Contrastive-LM, 2026; Convai Innovations, 2026; OpenAI, 2026; Microsoft, 2026). Their common interface makes a fast judgment available to an application or controller without asking a generative model to write a rationale, although their probabilities still require careful calibration and thresholding (Deußer et al., 2026; Porcedda, 2026; Rafe and Das, 2026), as do earlier fast judges and guard models (Kadavath et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2023; Inan et al., 2023). Like other fast models, they are mostly used before generation: cascades and routers escalate uncertain inputs, and fast-and-slow architectures invoke a stronger solver when the fast one falls short (Chen et al., 2024; Aggarwal et al., 2024; Ong et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2023; Bergamaschi Ganapini et al., 2025; Khandelwal et al., 2025).

2.3 Monitoring Reasoning During Generation

A few methods supervise a reasoning model while it generates. TrimR and FlashThink query a separate prompted LLM at reasoning boundaries, asking whether a conclusion has been reached or whether the thought so far suffices, and cut thinking short when it does (Lin et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2025). Meta-R1 and MetaCtrl let a meta-level component steer the reasoner, using a generative language model or a controller trained for concise reasoning (Dong et al., 2025; Wen et al., 2026). Each of these methods targets a single objective with a fixed question and action. SOMA instead pairs an S1 decision model with a shared controller, so that different objectives share one interface.

2.4 Inference-Time Control of Reasoning

We study two cases in which reasoning should change course after generation has begun. In overthinking, a model keeps revisiting an answer after reaching a useful conclusion (Chen et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2025; Sui et al., 2025); existing methods shorten reasoning by training the model or by stopping on trial-answer confidence, answer agreement, or hidden-state probes (Aggarwal and Welleck, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b; Fang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2026). In unanswerable-question settings, models may continue reasoning despite missing premises or an explicitly noticed flaw (Kirichenko et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2025; Ahn et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026); prior remedies use a hidden-state probe to trigger abstention guidance (Liu et al., 2026) or sequential statistical tests on uncertainty keywords to stop reasoning (Xie et al., 2026). These methods generally couple a scenario to a dedicated signal and action. SOMA instead expresses both cases as monitor specifications and reuses the same S1 model and controller, differing only in the behavior statement and predefined response.

3 SOMA

SOMA lets an S1 decision model supervise an S2 reasoning model while S2 is thinking. Following the separation of monitoring and control in human metacognition, it divides supervision into a scenario layer that defines what to supervise, an awareness layer in which S1 detects it, and a control layer that decides how to respond with a single rule shared by all scenarios (Figure 2). Each layer can be replaced on its own: a new objective only adds a scenario specification, and a different S1 model plugs in through the same interface.

Throughout this paper, QQ denotes the task and HtH_{t} the reasoning text that S2 has written after tt thinking tokens.

3.1 Scenario Layer: What to Supervise

A supervision objective is specified by a monitor m=(sm,rm,am)m=(s_{m},r_{m},a_{m}), consisting entirely of natural-language and predefined text.

Statement sms_{m}.

The statement describes the reasoning behavior to watch for, and it is the only part of the monitor that S1 sees. Statements follow a common pattern: X has appeared in the reasoning, but S2 is still doing Y. This form has two advantages. Both parts can be read off the visible text, unlike the correctness of an answer, and the statement stops being true once S2 changes its behavior, so S1’s later judgments show whether an intervention has taken effect.

Reminder rmr_{m}.

The reminder is a short message inserted into S2’s reasoning. Rather than issuing a command, it points to the possible problem and asks S2 to judge whether its current activity is useful, leaving the decision to S2.

Takeover action ama_{m}.

The takeover action is predefined text that ends thinking and steers the response, for example towards a final answer or a refusal. S2 still writes the final content after a takeover.

Because a monitor is plain text, adding a scenario requires neither training nor any change to the other two layers. The same form could also describe a reasoning trace that starts to comply with a jailbreak request.

3.2 Awareness Layer: S1 as an Observer

S1 is queried at regular pauses while S2 is thinking. At each pause, it receives the task, the reasoning so far and the statement, and returns

pt=S1⁡(Q,Ht,sm)∈[0,1],p_{t}=\mathrm{S1}(Q,H_{t},s_{m})\in[0,1],

the probability that the statement holds. This interface is the only requirement on S1: any decision model that maps a text state and a natural-language statement to a probability can fill the role. It also sees only text written by S2. Inserted reminders and the system prompt are hidden from it, so its judgment always concerns S2’s own behavior.

Pauses occur every XX thinking tokens. To avoid reading a half-written line, S2 first continues to the next line break and pauses there. Because S1 returns a single probability rather than generated text, each scan is one short call. When the reasoning exceeds S1’s input limit, the task is kept in full and the earliest part of the reasoning is dropped.

3.3 Control Layer: Remind First, Take Over on Persistent Evidence

The controller turns S1’s judgments into evidence on the log-odds scale and accumulates it as a one-sided cumulative sum:

S←max⁡{0,S+logit⁡(pt)−logit⁡(0.5)}.S\leftarrow\max\bigl\{0,\;S+\operatorname{logit}(p_{t})-\operatorname{logit}(0.5)\bigr\}.

A scan with pt>0.5p_{t}>0.5 raises SS, a scan with pt<0.5p_{t}<0.5 lowers it toward zero, and a scan with pt=0.5p_{t}=0.5 leaves it unchanged; SS never drops below zero.

This rule follows the one-sided cumulative-sum test for detecting a persistent change (Page, 1954). Since S1 reports the probability that the statement holds, logit⁡(pt)−logit⁡(0.5)\operatorname{logit}(p_{t})-\operatorname{logit}(0.5) is the evidence of one scan for the statement against even odds, and summing log-odds treats successive scans as separate pieces of evidence. A confident scan therefore counts more than a doubtful one, an isolated high score is absorbed by later low ones, and only a behavior that S1 keeps observing drives SS upward.

The controller responds in two stages (Algorithm 1). When SS first becomes positive, an episode begins: SOMA inserts the reminder rmr_{m} at the pause and resets SS to zero. S2 then continues and decides for itself how to respond. From this point SS accumulates only evidence gathered after the reminder. If it reaches a threshold hh, the controller executes the takeover action ama_{m}; if it falls back to zero first, the episode ends, and a later rise of SS above zero starts a new one with a new reminder.

The two stages differ in cost and reversibility. A reminder leaves S2 in charge and costs only a few tokens, whereas a takeover cannot be undone by S2. SOMA therefore takes over only when the behavior persists after S2 has been given a chance to stop, and it bases this decision on what S1 observes S2 doing after the reminder, not on what S2 says in reply. To make S2 attend to reminders, a single fixed system prompt, shared by all scenarios, tells S2 that a monitor may insert reminders into its reasoning.

3.4 Threshold Calibration

A takeover is the one intervention S2 cannot recover from. Once thinking is cut off and the response is steered, a mistaken takeover becomes a wrong answer or a false refusal, whereas a mistaken reminder can simply be dismissed by S2. The threshold hh therefore decides how much post-reminder evidence SOMA requires before it accepts this risk.

No single threshold suits every setting: the evidence that SS accumulates depends on how sharply S1 separates cases in which the statement holds from those in which it does not (Deußer et al., 2026), on how S2 responds to reminders, and on how often a monitor’s behavior occurs and what a mistaken takeover costs. SOMA therefore calibrates a separate threshold for each combination of S1, S2 and monitor.

Calibration takes place before deployment, on a small set 𝒞\mathcal{C} of representative tasks for the target scenario. On these tasks, SOMA under each candidate threshold h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H} is compared with S2 running under the same system prompt without any intervention, so that every difference between the two is caused by the intervention. Let c0​(q)∈{0,1}c_{0}(q)\in\{0,1\} indicate whether S2 handles task qq correctly on its own, and ch​(q)c_{h}(q) whether it does so under SOMA with threshold hh. In overthinking, a task is handled correctly when the final answer is correct; for unanswerable questions, when S2 abstains on an unanswerable question or correctly answers an answerable one. Harm thus covers both answers spoiled by an early takeover and false refusals. We measure the harm of a threshold as the number of tasks that the intervention turns from correct to wrong:

L⁡(h)=∑q∈𝒞c0​(q)​(1−ch​(q)),L(h)=\sum_{q\in\mathcal{C}}c_{0}(q)\,\bigl(1-c_{h}(q)\bigr),

and choose the smallest threshold whose harm is within a tolerance δ≥0\delta\geq 0 of the lowest achievable harm:

h∗=min⁡{h∈ℋ:L⁡(h)≤minh′∈ℋ⁡L⁡(h′)+δ}.h^{*}=\min\Bigl\{h\in\mathcal{H}:\ L(h)\leq\min_{h^{\prime}\in\mathcal{H}}L(h^{\prime})+\delta\Bigr\}.

A smaller threshold takes over earlier and saves more computation, so the rule selects the most aggressive threshold whose harm stays within the tolerance; δ\delta sets how much harm is acceptable in exchange for savings. Once chosen, the threshold stays fixed during use.

4 Experiments

4.1 Setup

Scenarios.

We evaluate SOMA on overthinking, where the goal is to cut redundant verification without lowering accuracy, and on unanswerable questions, where S2 should abstain when a problem lacks necessary information or has contradictory conditions and solve it otherwise. Both scenarios use the same S1 model, controller and system prompt, and differ only in their monitors (Table 1).

Models.

We use Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025) and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B (Guo et al., 2025) as S2, served with vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) in thinking mode with the recommended sampling settings (temperature 0.6, top-pp 0.95, and top-kk 20 for Qwen3-8B) and a limit of 32,768 generated tokens. Every method samples each question once. S1 is Jev (Almeida, 2026; TypeSafe AI, 2026), accessed through its API.

Benchmarks.

For overthinking, we use GSM8K (1,319 questions; Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH-500 (500; Hendrycks et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024), AIME 2024–2025 (60; Mathematical Association of America, 2025), AMC 2023 (40; Mathematical Association of America, 2023) and GPQA-Diamond (198; Rein et al., 2024). For unanswerable questions, we use the test sets of SUM (284 unanswerable and 284 answerable questions; Song et al., 2025) and UMWP (300 and 300; Sun et al., 2024), following Liu et al. (2026). Mathematical answers are checked with Math-Verify (Kydlíček, 2025), and abstentions are identified with the rule of Liu et al. (2026).

Implementation.

S2 pauses every X=256X=256 thinking tokens, continuing to the next line break for at most 128 further tokens. The state passed to S1 is limited to 2,048 tokens, and a fixed system prompt shared by both scenarios tells S2 that a monitor may insert reminders (Appendix A).

Calibration.

Thresholds are calibrated as in §3.4 with δ=0\delta=0 on one easier and one harder set of 100 questions per scenario, disjoint from all test sets (Appendix C). The resulting thresholds are h=0.25h=0.25 (Qwen3-8B) and h=1.5h=1.5 (R1-Distill-Llama-8B) for overthinking, and h=4h=4 and h=3h=3 for unanswerable questions.

Single-run readout.

Since a takeover ends generation, we run SOMA once with reminders but no takeovers and read off the outcome under each threshold hh at the first pause where the post-reminder evidence reaches hh, both for calibration and at test time (Appendix B).

Baselines.

All methods share the decoding settings, generation limit, data, and scoring above; prompts are method-specific. We report Vanilla (thinking mode). For overthinking, we compare with budget forcing (BF; Muennighoff et al., 2025), DEER (Yang et al., 2026) and Dynasor-CoT (Fu et al., 2025b; Fu et al., 2025a). For unanswerable questions, we compare with DEER, Dynasor-CoT, the AbstentionBench prompt (Kirichenko et al., 2025), statistical early stopping (SES; Xie et al., 2026) and Answering the Unanswerable (AtU; Liu et al., 2026), which uses a hidden-state probe trained for each S2 model. Parameters that require tuning are selected with each paper’s own procedure on the same calibration sets as SOMA’s thresholds (Appendix E).

Metrics.

For overthinking, we report accuracy and the mean number of S2 tokens (Tok), counting thinking and answer tokens as well as extra tokens a method generates, such as trial answers. For unanswerable questions, we report the abstention rate on unanswerable questions (Abs), the accuracy (Acc) and false-abstention rate (FA) on answerable questions, and Tok. For SOMA, token accounting follows the readout in Appendix B. Averages (Avg) weight each benchmark by its number of questions.

4.2 Main Results

Overthinking.

Table 2 shows that SOMA shortens reasoning while preserving and slightly improving accuracy on average. It reduces generated tokens by 36% on Qwen3-8B and 16% on R1-Distill-Llama-8B, and raises average accuracy from 91.0% to 91.3% and from 84.4% to 84.8%. Weighting each benchmark equally, which removes the dominance of GSM8K, the gains are 0.8 and 3.4 points, and SOMA has the highest such average on R1-Distill-Llama-8B (72.0% vs. 69.4% for Dynasor-CoT). SOMA exceeds Vanilla on six of the ten model-benchmark combinations, with the largest gains on the hardest benchmarks: on AIME, accuracy rises from 66.7% to 73.3% on Qwen3-8B and from 36.7% to 45.0% on R1-Distill-Llama-8B, and on GPQA-Diamond it improves by 3.5 and 4.5 points. On the remaining combinations the differences are small, at most 1.4 points except for two questions on AMC 2023 with Qwen3-8B. By contrast, DEER saves more tokens but lowers average accuracy by 2.9 and 6.3 points, and BF stays close to Vanilla in accuracy but saves only 8% and 5% of the tokens. Dynasor-CoT keeps accuracy but saves only 6% of the tokens on Qwen3-8B; on R1-Distill-Llama-8B it saves 13% with accuracy comparable to SOMA.

Unanswerable questions.

Table 3 shows that SOMA substantially improves abstention on unanswerable questions while shortening reasoning. On Qwen3-8B, it raises average abstention from 70.5% to 87.2%, the highest among all methods, and reduces tokens by 32%. On R1-Distill-Llama-8B, it raises abstention from 38.2% to 59.4% with the largest token reduction of all methods (48%). The gains are largest on SUM, the harder benchmark, where abstention rises from 60% to 87% and from 28% to 70%. On SUM, SOMA exceeds AtU on Qwen3-8B (87% vs. 83%) and is one percentage point lower on R1-Distill-Llama-8B (70% vs. 71%), even though AtU trains a probe on SUM for each S2 model, whereas SOMA treats S2 as a black box and needs no training. These gains come with a moderate rise in false abstentions on answerable questions, from 2.4% to 8.0% and from 2.1% to 4.8% on average. On UMWP, SOMA raises the abstention of Qwen3-8B from 81% to 88%. For R1-Distill-Llama-8B, it keeps accuracy and false abstention unchanged while cutting tokens by 59%, but abstention stays close to Vanilla (49% vs. 48%). Across both scenarios and both S2 models, SOMA lies on the token–quality Pareto frontier (Figure 3), the only method to do so in all four settings.

4.3 Ablation Study

We study the components of the control layer on a fixed subset of the test sets (Table 4); Appendix D varies the scan interval. All variants share the S1 model, monitors and system prompt.

Reminders and takeovers.

Remind-only inserts reminders but never takes over (h=∞h=\infty). In overthinking, reminders alone already shorten reasoning (by 16% on Qwen3-8B and 3% on R1-Distill-Llama-8B) without lowering accuracy, and adding takeovers brings total savings to 42% and 15%. For unanswerable questions, reminders alone leave abstention close to Vanilla, so the gain in abstention comes from the takeover. No reminder skips the first stage: it accumulates evidence from the first pause and takes over without reminding S2, using its own calibrated threshold. For unanswerable questions it performs similarly to SOMA. In overthinking, the threshold calibrated without a reminder is much higher, and the variant saves about half as many tokens on Qwen3-8B (22% vs. 42%) with accuracy 1.6 percentage points higher; on R1-Distill-Llama-8B it saves 11% against 15% at similar accuracy.

Case studies.

Appendix F shows both stages at work. The typical success is a model that notices a problem but does not act on it: on a SUM question whose denominator has no last term, Qwen3-8B names the gap at once, yet without SOMA it answers under an assumption after 6,148 tokens; under SOMA, S1 keeps observing the same search after the reminder, and the takeover turns S2’s own doubt into an abstention after 1,392 tokens. In overthinking, a takeover keeps a confirmed answer, cutting 21,665 tokens to 1,120. The reminder alone can also suffice: R1-Distill-Llama-8B guesses a missing number on a SUM question without SOMA, but after the reminder it re-checks the problem and abstains (4,903 to 1,149 tokens).

5 Conclusion

We introduced SOMA, in which an S1 decision model continuously monitors S2’s reasoning for a behavior described in natural language, reminds S2 when it appears, and takes over only if the behavior persists after the reminder. SOMA requires neither training nor access to S2’s internal states, since S1 reads only the visible reasoning text. On overthinking, SOMA cut reasoning tokens by 36% and 16% on the two S2 models without lowering average accuracy, and on unanswerable questions it raised abstention by 17 and 21 points.

Because objectives are written in natural language and S1 reads only visible text, adding a new objective requires only a monitor statement, a reminder and a takeover action, with no change to S2. S1 decision models can therefore serve as a general supervision layer that accompanies reasoning rather than gating it, and in future work the same layer can take on new objectives such as jailbreak defense or agent monitoring.

Limitations

Scope of the evaluation.

SOMA is designed as a general framework: a new objective needs only a monitor statement, a reminder and a takeover action, so the same layers could address other problems that surface in the reasoning, such as defending against jailbreaks. Due to time constraints, we evaluate only two scenarios, overthinking and unanswerable questions, both centered on mathematical and scientific reasoning, with two 8B reasoning models and one monitor per scenario. How well SOMA works in other scenarios and domains, with larger S2 models, and with several monitors running jointly remains to be tested.

A single S1 model.

All experiments use Jev, a hosted proprietary model whose behavior may change across versions. The framework only requires the S1 interface, but we test no other S1 model in the main experiments. The results therefore do not establish which other S1 models can fill the role.

Cost of S1 calls.

Jev is accessed through a paid API, and SOMA queries it at every pause. Our results come from the single-run readout (Appendix B); reported tokens cover S2 only, and we do not measure wall-clock latency. As mature open-source S1 models become available, S1 could be deployed on the same hardware as S2, removing the API cost and the network round trip.

Irreversible interventions.

A takeover cannot be undone by S2. Although thresholds are chosen to limit harm on calibration data, SOMA raises false abstentions on answerable questions, and a mistaken takeover in overthinking fixes an answer that S2 might still have corrected.

Broader Impact

SOMA lowers the cost of supervising a reasoning model: an objective is written as a natural-language statement rather than a task-specific signal or a trained probe, and S1 reads only the visible reasoning. This could make oversight of long reasoning and agent trajectories practical for users without access to model internals, including for safety objectives such as detecting jailbreak attempts. The same mechanism carries risks. A takeover overrides the model’s own reasoning, so a poorly written statement or a badly calibrated threshold can systematically suppress valid answers. Relying on a hosted S1 also sends the model’s reasoning to a third-party service, which matters when the reasoning contains private data; a locally deployed open-source S1 would avoid this.

Appendix A Implementation Details

A.1 Models and Decoding

The S2 models are Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025) and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B (Guo et al., 2025), and Jev (Almeida, 2026; TypeSafe AI, 2026) is the only S1 model. Every method samples each question once with a generation limit of 32,768 tokens and the recommended decoding settings of each model: temperature 0.6 and top-pp 0.95, with top-kk 20 for Qwen3-8B. Mathematical answers are scored with Math-Verify (Kydlíček, 2025), GPQA-Diamond uses its official answer labels, SUM and UMWP use their official answerability labels, and abstentions are identified with the rule of Liu et al. (2026). SOMA and its variants use the fixed system prompt shared by both scenarios:

“While you think, a monitor may insert a <reminder>. When you see one, follow its instruction briefly inside your reasoning, then continue as you judge best.”

A.2 S1 State and Scan Schedule

At each scan, Jev receives the complete task and the S2 text in fields named “Task: QQ” and “Reasoning so far: HH”, separated by blank lines. The state is limited to 2,048 tokens under the Qwen3 tokenizer, after reserving room for the longest monitor statement. The complete task is retained, and the oldest part of HH is removed when the limit is exceeded. SOMA scans only while S2 is thinking. After every 256 thinking tokens, S2 continues to the next line break and pauses there; if no line break appears within 128 further tokens, it pauses without one. Reminders are inserted at the pause as a separate paragraph wrapped in <reminder> tags. They become part of S2’s context but are excluded from HH on later scans.

A.3 Takeovers

In overthinking, a takeover appends the model’s end-of-thinking delimiter and “**Final Answer**”, and S2 then writes at most 64 tokens. For an unanswerable question, it inserts the fixed conclusion “The problem is missing necessary information or has contradictory conditions, so it cannot be answered as stated.”, closes thinking, pre-fills “\boxed{I don’t know.}”, and allows S2 512 tokens for the reason.

Appendix B Single-Run Readout

Since a takeover ends generation, running every candidate threshold separately would multiply the cost of calibration by the size of the grid. We therefore run SOMA once in an observe-remind mode: reminders are inserted as usual, but no takeover is executed, and every scan is recorded. A trial takeover is recorded whenever the post-reminder SS first reaches a candidate threshold. The outcome under a threshold hh is the trial at the first pause where S≥hS\geq h, or the full trajectory if hh is never reached; h=∞h=\infty gives the remind-only variant. Up to the first reminder, SOMA coincides with S2 running under the same system prompt without intervention, so each such trajectory is generated once and SOMA continues from it. The same readout, with the frozen thresholds, is used for evaluation. At the pause where the takeover would have happened, the outcome and token count are computed as follows.

  • •

    Overthinking. We append the takeover text and let S2 write its final answer (at most 64 tokens). The answer is scored as usual. The token count is the number of tokens S2 wrote before the pause, plus the takeover text and the final answer.

  • •

    Unanswerable questions. The pre-filled refusal determines the outcome, so the trial is scored as an abstention. S2 then writes the reason (at most 512 tokens), and the token count is the number of tokens S2 wrote before the pause, plus the tokens of the generated reason.

Appendix C Calibration and Ablation Data

The calibration sets are disjoint from all test questions, and each scenario has an easier and a harder set of 100 questions. For overthinking, the easier set consists of MATH training problems sampled to match the difficulty distribution of MATH-500, and the harder set of problems from AIME 2020–2023. For unanswerable questions, the easier set contains 50 answerable and 50 unanswerable problems drawn from the original UMWP release but excluded from its test split, and the harder set contains 50 SUM training pairs, each consisting of an answerable problem and its unanswerable counterpart. We search ℋ={0.25,0.5,0.75,1,1.5,2,2.5,3,4,6,8,12}\mathcal{H}=\{0.25,0.5,0.75,1,1.5,2,2.5,3,4,6,8,12\} with δ=0\delta=0. Table 5 reports the calibration outcomes at the selected thresholds of SOMA and of the No-reminder variant.

The ablations in §4.3 use a fixed subset of the test sets, selected by hashing question identifiers: all of MATH-500 (500 questions) and AIME (60) for overthinking, and 100 SUM pairs and 100 answerable plus 100 unanswerable UMWP questions for unanswerable questions.

Appendix D Scan Interval

Scanning more often lets SOMA notice a behavior earlier (Table 6). Halving the interval to X=128X=128 increases savings in both scenarios (to 48% and 19% in overthinking, and to 36% and 51% for unanswerable questions) and raises abstention on R1-Distill-Llama-8B from 60% to 63%, at the cost of about 1.5–2 times as many S1 calls. Doubling it to X=512X=512 roughly halves the S1 calls but reduces savings and, on R1-Distill-Llama-8B, abstention, while slightly raising overthinking accuracy on Qwen3-8B through fewer takeovers. The interval thus trades monitoring cost against responsiveness, and X=256X=256 lies between the two.

Appendix E Baselines

We reproduce all baselines from their released code, following the specifications reported in their papers. Where a method has parameters that must be tuned, we select them with the procedure of its paper on the same calibration sets used for SOMA’s thresholds (Appendix C), separately for each S2 model and scenario. All baselines share the task prompts, decoding settings, data and generation limit of §4.1, while keeping their own intervention prompts.

Budget forcing (BF) (Muennighoff et al., 2025).

A length-control method that caps thinking at a fixed token budget: once the budget is reached, thinking is cut off and the model is prompted to give its final answer. The budget is selected on the calibration sets.

DEER (Yang et al., 2026).

An early-exit method based on the reasoner’s own confidence. At reasoning transitions such as “Wait”, the reasoner writes a trial answer, and thinking ends once its confidence in that answer is high enough, using the threshold of the paper.

Dynasor-CoT (Fu et al., 2025b; Fu et al., 2025a).

An early-exit method based on answer consistency. At fixed intervals, an intermediate answer is elicited and then discarded, and the method exits once several consecutive answers agree and show no hesitation. The probing interval and the number of consecutive answers are selected on the calibration sets.

Answering the Unanswerable (Liu et al., 2026).

A white-box method that monitors S2’s hidden states with a linear probe trained for each model. When the probe indicates that the question is unanswerable, it inserts guidance that leads S2 to abstain. We use the released probe weights and select the probe’s decision threshold on the calibration sets.

Statistical early stopping (Xie et al., 2026).

A method that tracks how often uncertainty keywords appear in the reasoning and stops when a statistical test finds that they appear more often than is typical for answerable questions. Its statistics for answerable questions are estimated on the answerable questions of the calibration sets, and the remaining settings follow the paper. The paper proposes a renewal and a maxwise stopping rule; we report the renewal rule, the stronger of the two in our runs. Because the method does not specify an action after stopping, it uses our refusal takeover.

AbstentionBench prompt (Kirichenko et al., 2025).

A prompt-only baseline that adds the official AbstentionBench system prompt, which encourages the model to abstain when a question cannot be answered.

Appendix F Case Studies

This appendix shows how SOMA behaves on individual questions, with four successful and two failed cases. All cases come from the main test run. For each case we show the question, the vanilla response, and SOMA’s monitoring trace. At every scan the trace lists the position in S2 tokens, S1’s probability pp that the monitor statement holds, the evidence after the update, and the action.

F.1 Successful cases

The S2 model notices the ambiguity before the reminder but keeps resolving it by assumption. The check reminder does not change this: S2 decides that “many” means two pieces. S1 keeps observing the same behaviour (p=0.87p=0.87, 0.900.90), the post-reminder evidence reaches hh after two scans, and the takeover ends the episode. The reason is written by S2 and names the missing quantity.

This is the “knowing but not acting” pattern that motivates SOMA: vanilla names the missing endpoint in its first paragraph and still produces a definite answer. With SOMA, S2 again searches for an implied endpoint after the reminder; S1’s evidence grows on every scan, and the takeover turns the doubt S2 already expressed into an abstention.

Here the check reminder does what it asks for: S2 re-examines the problem, concludes that information is missing, and ends its reasoning by itself. Such cases are the minority in our runs. On the full SUM test set the reminder alone raises R1’s abstention rate only from 28% (Vanilla) to 30%, and most of SOMA’s gain comes from the takeover.

After the reminder, S2 states that its checks have confirmed the answer, yet it starts another round (“Let me just make sure …”). This is exactly the observable symptom of the monitor statement. S1 scores it with p=0.91p=0.91 at the next scan, and the takeover keeps the confirmed answer. Vanilla’s extra verification adds no information; its numerical check even introduces a spurious doubt.

F.2 Failure cases

S1 judges the visible text correctly: an answer has been reached and S2 is re-checking it without naming a concern. But S1 does not, by design, judge whether the answer is right, and this particular check would have found the error. This is the residual risk of early exit. The reset makes the takeover wait for evidence after the reminder, and the calibrated hh keeps such cases rare.

S2 has already found the intended factor, but it keeps questioning whether answer options are missing. The monitor statement describes this visible behavior truthfully, and moderate probabilities (p=0.64p=0.64 to 0.720.72) accumulate over five scans until they reach h=4h=4. S1 judges what S2 does, not whether the information S2 misses is really necessary. False refusals therefore arise when S2 voices unwarranted doubts.

Summary.

In the successful cases, S1 detects a persistent, observable symptom: an assumption made despite missing information, or verification of an answer that is already confirmed. The reminder occasionally resolves the case by itself; otherwise, the evidence S1 collects after the reminder triggers the takeover. The failures have two distinct causes. The first is a check that would have been productive, which S1 cannot recognize without judging correctness. The second is S2 voicing doubts that S1 correctly observes but that are unwarranted.
